en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Non-Proliferation, Concerning the Question on Inference.
2. The Question on the State of One Whose Taints Are Exhausted “Venerable Nāgasena, you say:
‘For a householder who has attained Arahantship, there are two destinations and no other: either he goes forth on that very day, or he attains final Nibbāna.’”
"That day cannot be allowed to pass. "Venerable Nāgasena,
if on that day he were not to obtain a teacher or a preceptor, or an alms-bowl and robes,
would that Arahant ordain himself, or would he let the day pass, or would another [ordain him]?"
“Would some Arahant possessing psychic power come and ordain him, or would he attain final Nibbāna?
“Great King, that Arahant would not ordain himself; if he were to ordain himself, he would fall into theft.
Nor would he wait for the day to pass; whether another Arahant arrives or not, [he would act] at that very moment.”
“...he might attain final Nibbāna on that very day.
“In that case, venerable Nāgasena, the state of peace inherent in Arahantship has been lost, since it results in the taking away of life for one who has attained it.

“The layman’s mark, Great King, is unstable. Because of the instability of that mark, a layman who has attained Arahantship either goes forth into homelessness on that very same day or attains final Nibbāna.”
“Great King, that is not a fault of arahantship; rather, this is a fault of the householder’s mark, namely, the weakness of that mark.

Just as food, Great King, which sustains the life-span and protects the life of all beings, takes away life from one with a diseased stomach who has weak digestion because it does not digest—it is not a fault of the food, Great King, but a fault of the stomach, namely, the weakness of its fire.”

In the same way, Great King, when a householder who has attained Arahantship while wearing the marks of a layman finds those marks to be weak, he either goes forth on that very day or attains final Nibbāna.
This, Great King, is not a fault of Arahantship; it is a fault of the layman’s marks themselves, namely their weakness.
Or again, Great King, just as a small blade of grass, when a heavy stone is placed upon it, breaks and falls because of its weakness; so too, Great King, is this case.

In the same way, Great King, a householder who has attained arahantship, being unable to maintain that state of arahantship under the outward marks of a layman, either goes forth into homelessness on that very day or attains final Nibbāna.

Or again, Great King, just as a man who is weak, feeble, of low birth, and of meager merit, having obtained a vast and great kingdom, falls, perishes, and declines in an instant, being unable to sustain his sovereignty; so it is with him.

“In the same way, Great King, a layman who has attained Arahatship is unable to maintain that state of Arahatship under the outward marks of a householder; for that reason, on that very day, he either goes forth into homelessness or attains Parinibbāna.
“Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it.
The second question, concerning the state of one whose taints are exhausted.
